questions.stem: Potassium permanganate is a purple solid that is soluble in water. start after a short time A crystal of potassium permanganate is placed in a beaker containing water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a short time, the crystal becomes smaller and the liquid at the bottom of the beaker becomes purple. Which statement explains this observation? A the crystal condenses in the water B the crystal dissolves in the water C the crystal evaporates in the water D the crystal melts in the water

parts.label: b
parts.text: The beaker is left until there is no further change in the appearance of the liquid.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Which statement describes the final appearance of the liquid? A all of the liquid is purple B none of the liquid is purple C only the bottom half of the liquid is purple D only the top half of the liquid is purple

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Which process causes this change in appearance? B crystallisation A condensation C diffusion D evaporation

parts.label: c
parts.text: The formula of potassium permanganate is $ \mathrm{K M n O_{4}} $ How many different elements are there in potassium permanganate? A 3 B 4 C 6 D 7

questions.stem: The diagram shows part of the Periodic Table, with elements represented by the letters L, M, Q, R and T. The letters in the diagram represent elements but are not their chemical symbols.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the letter from the diagram that represents a noble gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Elements L and M are in the same group. State why they have similar chemical reactions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An atom of element Q has 31 protons. Use this information to explain how you can determine the number of protons in an atom of element R.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the formula of the ion that produces the red flame.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the cream precipitate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the white solid.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student uses a clean metal wire in the flame test.

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: State why the wire should be clean when used in the flame test.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: The table lists properties of some metals. Add ticks ( $ \surd $ ) to the table to show the two properties needed in a metal wire used in a flame test.

questions.stem: A student uses this apparatus to investigate the colours in four different inks, A, B, C and D.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two mistakes the student made when setting up his experiment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another student does the experiment but does not make any mistakes. The diagram shows her results.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: State how many colours ink D contains.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: State which of the inks tested could be mixed together to make ink D.

parts.label: b-iii

questions.stem: In 1937 an airship full of hydrogen gas flew from Germany to America.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Which property of hydrogen makes it a suitable gas to use in an airship? A colourless B insoluble in water C low density D no smell

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why helium is now used in airships instead of hydrogen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hydrogen is used to manufacture ammonia, $ \mathrm{N H_{3}} $ Hydrogen is reacted with nitrogen using an iron catalyst.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: Give a chemical equation for this reaction.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: State why a catalyst is used in this reaction.

questions.stem: The reactions of metals with water and with dilute sulfuric acid can be used to determine the order of reactivity of the metals. The table shows the reactions of four metals, W, X, Y and Z, with water and with dilute sulfuric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the order of reactivity of these metals?

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which metal, W, X, Y or Z, could be copper.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: State which metal, W, X, Y or Z, could be magnesium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A displacement reaction can also be used to decide the order of reactivity of two metals. State two observations made when an excess of magnesium powder is added to an aqueous solution of copper(II) sulfate.

questions.stem: Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide all have giant covalent structures. The diagram shows the structures of these three substances. diamond graphite silicon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why silicon dioxide has a high melting point.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why graphite conducts electricity.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why diamond is hard but graphite is soft.

questions.stem: Ethene $ \left( \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{4} \right) $ can be converted into chloroethene $ \left( \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{3} \mathrm{Cl} \right) $ in a two-stage process.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The first stage is to convert ethene into 1,2-dichloroethane, $ \mathrm{C_{2} H_{4} C l_{2}} $ Ethene is reacted with hydrogen chloride and oxygen. Complete the chemical equation for this reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In the second stage, 1,2-dichloroethane is converted into chloroethene. $\mathrm {C} _ {2} \mathrm {H} _ {4} \mathrm {C l} _ {2} \rightarrow \mathrm {C} _ {2} \mathrm {H} _ {3} \mathrm {C l} + \mathrm {H C l}$ This is a thermal decomposition reaction. State what is meant by the term thermal decomposition.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The diagram shows the displayed formula of chloroethene.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: State why chloroethene is described as an unsaturated compound.

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Describe a test to show that chloroethene is unsaturated.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the polymer formed from chloroethene.

questions.stem: Halon 1301 is a compound used in some fire extinguishers. Halon 1301 has the percentage composition by mass of C 8.05% Br 53.69% F 38.26%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show, by calculation, that the empirical formula of this compound is $ \mathrm{C B r F}_{3} $

parts.label: c
parts.text: The boiling point of Halon 1301 is $ - 5 8^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $. Explain why Halon 1301 has a low boiling point.

parts.label: b-i

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen required to react with 32 g of methane. $ [ M_{r} $ of methane=16]

parts.label: b
parts.text: The diagram shows methane burning in air. It also shows how the two gases formed are collected and tested.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: Explain why water collects in the U-tube.

parts.label: b-ii

parts.label: b-iii
parts.text: Explain the change in appearance of the limewater.

questions.stem: A student uses this apparatus to investigate the temperature change that occurs when ammonium nitrate is dissolved in water. She uses this method. put $ 1 0 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of water into the polystyrene cup and measure the initial temperature of the water add 8.00 g of ammonium nitrate and stir record the lowest temperature reached by the solution The table shows her results. Initial temperature of water in $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ 20.0 Lowest temperature of solution in $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $ 14.2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results of the experiment to explain what type of reaction is taking place when ammonium nitrate is added to water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the heat energy change, Q, is about 2400 J. [mass of 1.00 $ cm^{3} $ of solution = 1.00 g] [for the solution, c = 4.18 J/g/ $ ^{\circ} C $]

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to part (b) to calculate the enthalpy change, $ \Delta H $ , in kilojoules per mole of ammonium nitrate. [M $ _{r} $ of ammonium nitrate = 80.0] Include a sign in your answer.

questions.stem: A student uses this apparatus to investigate the rate of reaction between magnesium and an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid. She uses this method. use a graduated beaker to pour $ 50 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of dilute hydrochloric acid of concentration 2.00 mol/dm $ ^{3} $ into the conical flask add a piece of magnesium ribbon of mass 0.086 g to the acid and put the bung into the neck of the flask measure the total volume of gas collected every ten seconds until the reaction stops The table shows the student's results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plot the student's results on the grid.

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Draw a curve of best fit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment using 0.043 g of magnesium ribbon $ 5 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of 2.00 mol/dm $ ^{3} $ hydrochloric acid Draw, on the grid in part (a), the curve you would expect in this experiment. Label this curve Y.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: The student repeats the experiment again, using 0.086g of magnesium ribbon $ 5 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of $ 2. 0 0 \mathrm{m o l} / \mathrm{d m}^{3} $ hydrochloric acid a slightly higher temperature than the first experiment Draw, on the grid in part (a), the curve you would expect in this experiment. Label this curve Z.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The expected volume of gas produced in the first experiment is $ 8 6 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ Suggest why the volume collected is less than the expected volume.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The student uses a graduated beaker to measure the volume of dilute hydrochloric acid. Explain why it is not necessary to use a measuring cylinder in this experiment.

parts.label: e
parts.text: The ionic equation for the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid is $\mathrm {M g} (\mathrm {s}) + 2 \mathrm {H} ^ {+} (\mathrm {a q}) \rightarrow \mathrm {M g} ^ {2 +} (\mathrm {a q}) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} (\mathrm {g})$ Use the information in this equation, and the particle collision theory, to explain why the rate of reaction decreases during each of the experiments.

questions.stem: A salt can be made by reacting an acid with an insoluble base. The student uses this method. Stage 1 pour $ 5 0 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker Stage 2 warm the acid using a Bunsen burner Stage 3 add a small amount of copper(II) oxide to the warm acid and stir the mixture Stage 4 add further amounts of copper(II) oxide until copper(II) oxide is in excess Stage 5 filter the mixture Stage 6 obtain crystals from the filtrate A student has a sample of copper(II) oxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the acid is warmed in stage 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student would know that the copper(II) oxide is in excess in stage 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the mixture is filtered in stage 5.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the colour of the filtrate obtained in stage 5.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Describe how the student could obtain a pure, dry sample of hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals from the filtrate in stage 6.

parts.label: f
parts.text: The overall equation for the formation of hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide is $\mathrm {C u O (s)} + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {S O} _ {4} (\mathrm {a q}) + 4 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {I}) \rightarrow \mathrm {C u S O} _ {4}. 5 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {s})$

parts.label: f-i
parts.text: In an experiment, a student completely reacts 9.54 g copper(II) oxide. Show that the maximum possible mass of $ \mathrm{C u S O_{4}. 5 H_{2} O} $ crystals that can be obtained is about 30 g. $[ M _ {\mathrm {r}} \mathrm {o f C u O} = 7 9. 5 M _ {\mathrm {r}} \mathrm {o f C u S O} _ {4}. 5 \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} = 2 4 9. 5 ]$ Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.

parts.label: f-ii
parts.text: In this experiment, the actual yield of $ \mathrm{C u S O_{4}. 5 H_{2} O} $ crystals is 23.92 g. Calculate the percentage yield of $ \mathrm{C u S O_{4}. 5 H_{2}O} $
